title: Hosea 14:1–9
context: Hosea closes the book with a call to return. He urges Israel to return to the LORD and gives the people words of confession that renounce trust in Assyria, horses, and idols (14:1–3). The LORD answers with a promise to heal their waywardness and love them freely (14:4), and he pictures a restored Israel with images of dew, lily, olive tree, grain, vine, and the fragrance of Lebanon (14:5–7). The LORD then speaks to Ephraim about idols and likens himself to “a green cypress tree” (14:8). A closing wisdom saying invites readers to understand the ways of the LORD (14:9). Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as the LORD’s gracious invitation and promise of restoration, and both hold repentance and healing together. They differ mainly in how they relate the people’s return in 14:1–3 to the LORD’s healing in 14:4, as the notes on that verse explain. Versification: English 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1, and English 14:1–9 is Hebrew 14:2–10; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: Israel, return to the LORD your God; for you have fallen because of your sin.
verses.arminianNotes: “Israel, return to the LORD your God; for you have fallen because of your sin.” Arminian readers hear a sincere invitation addressed to a people who can, by grace, answer it; their fall is real, and so is the open door.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a genuine call to return, and they see Hosea’s summons as a means by which the LORD draws his people back to himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining honest confession of sin with hope, and as the hinge from the judgment of 13:16 to the promises that follow.

verses.text: Take words with you, and return to the LORD. Tell him, “Forgive all our sins, and accept that which is good; so we offer bulls as we vowed of our lips.
verses.arminianNotes: “Take words with you, and return to the LORD.” Arminian readers see grace that even supplies the words of repentance, inviting the people to pray, “Forgive all our sins, and accept that which is good”, and to offer what they have vowed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD providing the very prayer of confession. The offering of the lips is rendered in more than one way, and many readers compare “the fruit of lips” in Hebrews 13:15. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that true return is spoken, honest, and directed to the LORD’s forgiveness.

verses.text: Assyria can’t save us. We won’t ride on horses; neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, ‘Our gods!’ for in you the fatherless finds mercy.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people’s prayer continues, “Assyria can’t save us. We won’t ride on horses”. Arminian readers hear repentance as a real renunciation of false securities: foreign alliances, military power, and the work of their own hands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the confession turning from every rival trust to the LORD, ending with the reason “in you the fatherless finds mercy”. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as answering 12:1 and 13:2, and as confessing that mercy rests with the LORD alone.

verses.text: “I will heal their waywardness. I will love them freely; for my anger is turned away from them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will heal their waywardness. I will love them freely”. Arminian readers hear grace offered freely and received in repentance: the return of 14:1–3 is a real, grace-enabled response, and the LORD answers it with healing and a love Israel never earned. The Deuteronomy 10:16 box treats the wider question of how a call to return relates to God’s grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the unmerited initiative of grace: the LORD’s free love and healing are what produce and sustain the people’s return, so that even the turning of 14:1–3 is his gift. Shared ground: both traditions confess that this love is undeserved and that “my anger is turned away from them” by the LORD’s own mercy.

verses.text: I will be like the dew to Israel. He will blossom like the lily, and send down his roots like Lebanon.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will be like the dew to Israel.” Arminian readers hear the LORD’s gracious and refreshing presence, which turns the fleeting dew of 13:3 into a picture of steady blessing as Israel blossoms “like the lily”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD himself as the source of Israel’s renewed life, with roots sent down “like Lebanon”, a picture of stability after judgment. Shared ground: both traditions note the reversal of 13:3, where dew pictured passing away, and read the imagery as restoration that comes from the LORD.

verses.text: His branches will spread, and his beauty will be like the olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon.
verses.arminianNotes: “His branches will spread, and his beauty will be like the olive tree”. Arminian readers hear a restored people flourishing in beauty and fruitfulness, as the LORD’s love bears visible fruit in their common life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the growth, beauty, and fragrance of a people the LORD has restored, with the olive tree and the fragrance of Lebanon picturing lasting blessing. Shared ground: both traditions read the images as poetry of renewal rather than as a list of separate promises.

verses.text: Men will dwell in his shade. They will revive like the grain, and blossom like the vine. Their fragrance will be like the wine of Lebanon.
verses.arminianNotes: “Men will dwell in his shade. They will revive like the grain, and blossom like the vine.” Arminian readers hear restoration that reaches outward, with others finding shelter and life in a renewed Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the renewed people as a place of shelter and fruitfulness, the work of the LORD who promised to be like the dew in 14:5. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the fullness of the LORD’s restoration, with “the wine of Lebanon” crowning the imagery.

verses.text: Ephraim, what have I to do any more with idols? I answer, and will take care of him. I am like a green cypress tree; from me your fruit is found.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Ephraim, what have I to do any more with idols?” Arminian readers hear a final break with idolatry, whether as the LORD’s word to Ephraim or as an answer voiced for Ephraim, together with the promise “I answer, and will take care of him”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s tender care in the striking self-description “I am like a green cypress tree; from me your fruit is found”, which teaches that all of Israel’s fruitfulness comes from him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as answering the idolatry of 13:2 with the LORD’s own lasting provision.

verses.text: Who is wise, that he may understand these things? Who is prudent, that he may know them? For the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble in them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Who is wise, that he may understand these things?” Arminian readers hear a closing invitation to every reader to weigh Hosea’s words and walk in the LORD’s ways, since “the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble in them”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a wisdom saying that sums up the book, affirming that “the ways of the LORD are right” and that the same ways bring life to the righteous and stumbling to the rebellious. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a call to wise reading and faithful living, and as a fitting close to the book.
